utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, this is case number IT-05-87/1-PT, The Prosecutor versus Vlastimir Djordjevic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. I would like to have the appearances, from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I am Tom Hannis, Senior Trial Attorney on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor. I'm joined today by Patricia Neema, on my right, a trial attorney. On my far right is Mr. Scott Love, one of our interns, and to my left is our case manager, Iain Reid. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Dragoljub Djordjevic for Defence, with counsel for accused Djordjevic, and accompanied with me is my co-counsel, Mr. Djurdjic, and my legal assistant, Ms. Marie O'Leary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And welcome to you and good morning to you also, Mr. Djordjevic. I take it you can understand what we're saying through interpretation? That's very good. Ladies and gentlemen, we are here today for the Status Conference in this case. We had the last Status Conference on 22nd February, as I recall, and, as you know, we are supposed to meet in these conferences every 120 days. We have circulated an agenda for the meeting today. And let me quickly resume that on the agenda we have a brief review of the pending motions. We would like to look as number 2 on the agenda on other developments since the last Status Conference. As point number 3, I would like to be briefed on the level of disclosure, and -- and as number 4 on the agenda, I would like to have a discussion about the preparation for trial. And then we will have other matters. Is this acceptable to the parties or is there anything else that we need to include on the agenda?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Acceptable to me, Your Honour. I have nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's very good. And Mr. Djordjevic, I suppose you have it the same way since these issues were actually discussed at the 65 ter conference yesterday. But Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have nothing further to add for the time being, and we'll see in due course. Maybe we'll add something later on, but this will depend on these proceedings here today on this Status Conference. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. Well, let's get on with it then. The first point on the agenda is a review of the pending motions, and I believe that we have three or four pending motions on our table. One is the motion to amend the third amended joinder indictment, with annexes that we have received in due course -- in due time, sorry. And we are now in the process of examining the new amended indictments and the annexes, and I believe that we will be able to hand down our decision somewhere in the second week of July. I still need to consult the two other Judges in the Bench, but the aim, as far as the Chamber -- this Chamber is concerned, is to -- to be able to hand down a decision on the third amended joinder indictment somewhere in the second week of July. Then we have access motion -- Defence motion for access to all audio proceedings in Milutinovic, and that, needless to say, is something that the Milutinovic chamber will determine so that is beyond my jurisdiction. The third issue is the notice on the expert reports, under Rule 94 bis, and I have been told that there is an attempt by the Prosecution to seek leave to respond to that reply. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were going to seek leave to reply to the Defence response to the motion to -- regarding our motion to amend the indictment. That was the one they were going to seek leave to reply to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sorry, I was -- I overlooked that. But I think you have been instructed by our senior legal officer that you can just file your motion and then attach the -- the reply that you want to file.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. We can put those two together then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. The practice varies from chamber to chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No. We need to save time and there's no reason to waste time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So just come forward with your request and attach the reply to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We will do that. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And, finally, there is also a motion for access to materials in Milutinovic after 21st November 2007, and that, I guess, is also something that is with the Milutinovic Bench. That is as far as I can take it regarding the pending motions, and if none of the parties have anything to add, then I suggest we just move on. If we go to the second point of the agenda, I was looking to just have a look at what has happened since the last Status Conference, and I guess the most noticeable event is the filing of the Defence response to the expert reports, and we will have a look at that in due course. As for disclosure, I have been led to understand that -- that the disclosure is complete, both on Rule 66(A)(i) and 66(A)(ii). Is this correctly understood, Mr. Djordjevic, or are there still outgoing issues regarding disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are still waiting for certain confidential materials to be disclosed from us from Milutinovic, et al trial which have not been disclosed to the present day and I'd also like to say that, as far as certain decisions and rulings from November last year onwards that you have made, they were acted upon four months later so that in fact we received most of those exhibits quite recently. Of course, they have been disclosed, but as I say, we're still awaiting the confidential reports from the Milutinovic trial, so that's the only thing that I can tell you at present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. But as far as I have been informed, the delay in relation to those documents has to do with Rule 70 permissions so that is going to take the time that it is going to take and I suppose that the Milutinovic Trial Chamber is pressing ahead in order to obtain those permissions under Rule 70 as soon as they can. As soon as they get the permissions, you will be given the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is in conformity with the rules not a matter for discussion, but what I want to state is this, actually what I said a moment ago, that it will certainly have a reflection on the efficiency of the proceedings because the Defence needs a minimum amount of time to enable our client to have a fair trial and a proper Defence. That is what this is about. And the day before yesterday we were disclosed 38 audiotapes which we have to listen to, so you can imagine how much time and effort is needed for that alone, and I'd just like to indicate the fact that for our part, as far as the efficiency of the proceedings are concerned, there certainly won't be any problems expect for the need to be given a minimum amount of time to prepare Defence case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We understand your concerns, Mr. Djordjevic. The issue of the lack of resources is not something that is specific to the Defence. The Chamber also is struggling with -- with finding resources to -- to go through everything in time. But I can assure both parties that we will not press the speed of the trial preparation beyond what is required. I'll get back to this in a minute or two and you will see that we are now in a position to indicate with more precision when the trial is going to start, and I will have to say that this is something that I think all parties will have to respect and do their utmost to ensure that they are being ready for trial when the case is supposed to start. But I will get back to that in a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Judge, before we go on, I wanted to address one of your questions concerning the disclosure. You ask about 66(A)(ii). As far as the statements of witnesses, not all that disclosure has been made because we have not yet filed our list of witnesses we intend to call at trial pursuant to Rule 65 (E), I believe. So that process hasn't begun yet because we don't have a finalised witness list of witnesses to be called at trial. I didn't want to mislead the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Of course I'm aware of the fact that the final witness list has not been made yet but I hope you are in the process of putting that list together because you will be called to present it quite soon. Rule 68, I don't know if there's anything that needs to be said here. The Prosecution is under an ongoing obligation to disclose exculpatory material that is in its possession, and of course, if the Defence is aware of any exculpatory information that might be out there which is still not in the possession of the Prosecution, you are certainly called to notify the Prosecution of this, and then by way of communicating with the Prosecution to seek to get that information if you cannot get it yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is what we're doing, and for the moment I think we will succeed in obtaining all the exculpatory material which go to the advantage of the Defence, and as far as we're concerned we will do what is necessary for our part when the time comes and when we have all the exhibits that the Prosecution is going to disclose to us, because I consider that there is certainly more such material and I expect that to be disclosed, new exculpatory material, which would help the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Of course. But just that my experience is from other trials that frequently there is an issue that relates to the fact that the Prosecution is not in possession of exculpatory material that has been identified by the Defence, and this gives rise to friction time and again because the Prosecution is then saying that it not supposed to do the job of the Defence. That's why I'm saying if you are aware of material that could be exculpatory, then I suppose you can -- the first thing you would do is try to seek to obtain that information by yourself, but if you can't get it, then of course get in contact with the Prosecution to -- to encourage the Prosecution to actually seek it and put it forward to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. That was the intention of the Defence, and the main goal of the Defence is, of course that our client at all events, if he is responsible for any violations and if he is to be held accountable that he should be held accountable for only those acts that he should be held responsible for and not for others that he is not and should not be responsible for, so that is the principle of conduct of each and every Defence team and ours included, so we will insist upon that and we hope that we will meet with understanding on the part of the Prosecution when it comes to exculpatory material and exculpatory facts, exculpatory evidence and exhibits and the need to approach those materials, and so if the Defence cannot access them directly we'll certainly try to do so with the help of our colleagues across the way there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That is good to hear. If I then move on to the issue of inspection of materials in the possession of the Prosecution, I understand that there has been an inspection and that there was an issue regarding the provenance of some of the material identified by the Defence. But can I just ask the parties if this problem has been dealt with and is no longer an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is with great satisfaction that I should like to inform you that we have resolved the problem and that we had this first instance inspection yesterday, and if the need arises in the future, I'm quite sure that we're not going to encountered any problems in that regard, no problems from the Prosecution and Mr. Hannis and his associates. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djordjevic, and let me use this opportunity to thank you both parties for what appears to me to be good cooperation. Good cooperation between the parties is essential to the good development of the trial when we get there. So I'm very, very grateful to both parties for showing the will to cooperate and to get this trial ahead. Then there is an issue, if I move on, on motions to present evidence under Rule 92 bis and ter and quater. However I would expect had this to be a matter for the Trial Chamber in the end, so this is a bit premature to raise it at this point, but I have in my mind that I would like to invite the parties for a couple of 65 ter meetings in September just immediately prior to the trial and that's where perhaps we could have a look at these issues again in order to provide a maximum preparation for trial to the Trial Chamber. As regards notice of alibi and special defences under Rule 67, which is also something that we should pay attention to at this stage, I would like to repeat the agreement that we had last time, that notice of such special defences or alibi has to be given at least two weeks before the deadline for the Prosecution's submission of its pre-trial brief. Now, that leads me to the third point on the agenda; namely, the preparation for trial. Do you have a calendar before you, each of the parties? Does the registry have a calendar that we can borrow to the parties? Is there a calendar available on the screen somehow? Can you find it, because I need to go through some dates with you. Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could you show the Defence how to get there, so that we all have a calendar in front of us. Thank you very much, Madam Usher. The information that we have now is that given the developments in other cases before this Tribunal, and I'm talking about the Zupljanin, Stanisic trial and the Lukic trial, it seems as if we are next in line, so I think that it is very likely that I can say that -- sorry, in all likelihood this trial is the next new trial to start. You were informed at the 65 ter meeting that the trial certainly will start before the end of this year and that there was a possibility that it might start sometime before or after the 1st of November. The calculation that I have been able to make in respect of the time when there would be an available Trial Chamber is that this trial will start on Monday, the 13th of October, beginning by the pre-trial conference on that day, and the trial will start either on the following day or soon thereafter. This means that the Prosecution's pre-trial brief shall have to be submitted at least six weeks before that. And let me say one thing about the expected date for the commencement of the trial, that I just need to sort it out with the President, and as soon as I have done that, we will issue a Scheduling Order for the pre-trial conference to be held on Monday, the 13th of October or very shortly thereafter. If we then look at the calendar, I would propose that the Prosecution files its pre-trial brief on Friday, the 22nd of August. This is I don't know how many weeks ahead from now, but I would imagine that it would give the Prosecution enough time to -- to get it ready. If you are being given the Trial Chamber's decision on the third amended indictment no later than Friday, the 11th of July, then you have, one, two, three, four, five, six weeks after that to prepare and submit your pre-trial brief. And given the limited scope of the substantial changes that you have made in the new indictment, I think that it is not unreasonable. But let me hear your opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I appreciate that. I was going to start out making a request for mid September but now I see this trial date may be mid October, I would like to ask for something a little beyond the 22nd of August and actually I will go straight to my target date, Your Honour. I would like to ask for Monday, the 1st of September. The reason I say that is back in February when we had the last 65 ter and Status Conference at that time I think we still had a hope and belief in the MOS case, Milutinovic et al, that we would finish the evidence before the end of March. As it turned out we didn't finish evidence until the 22nd or 23rd of May so that put us basically seven weeks behind where we thought we would be at this time. As you know, Judge, our final written briefs in the MOS case are due on the 8th of July with oral arguments on the 22nd. Myself and the team working on that case are pretty fully engaged on that process as you might imagine, it being almost a two-year trial with over 240 witnesses called and I don't know how many thousand exhibits we have in evidence. I know that's pressing the deadline, but from my conversation with Defence counsel yesterday about the possible dates we might be looking at, I think they too are interested in having as much time as possible. Now one thing I would propose to Your Honour, to speed the process and hopefully make the trial more efficient, was if you would be willing to give us until the 1st of September to file our pre-trial brief, I think we can file our witness list and our exhibit list prior to the 1st of September, because that's something we can get done more quickly and easily than writing the pre-trial brief. Another problem is, after two years, much of my staff on this case are fairly exhausted and people have arranged for vacations the first two weeks or so in August with non-refundable tickets and reservations in hot spots like Croatia, et cetera where it's hard to replace it. So that just a personal me I throw in as well, Your Honour. I'm basically asking for ten days beyond what you proposed. That's my pitch. And if I misstated the Defence position, I'll let them address it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Hannis. I must say that as much compassion I have for the staff situation in your team, I am unwilling to deviate. And the reason why I'm unwilling is that I don't want to see this trial being led into the almost unavoidable slip of time that we always experience. If I'm going to promise the President that this trial can and will start on Monday, the 13th of October, then there is no leeway given for us to change the dates of submission. You will notice that Friday, the 22nd of August is actually seven weeks before the opening statement and the pre-trial conference. But I think, given the experience that we have, that it is still wise to maintain the 22nd of August as the date in which we ask the Prosecution to file its pre-trial brief. It's one week after the recess, and, as I say, it's seven weeks after the submission of the handing down of the decision on the indictment. And, again, let me stress that if you get the decision, if you receive the decision by the Trial Chamber on the third -- on the recent amended indictment as late as on Friday, the 11th of July, I hope it might be before, but that's the latest date, then the substantive changes that have been proposed is really not very dramatic, to put it mildly. We're speaking about the inclusion of two or three incidents covering, I think, 18 new murders, but it doesn't change the nature and the scope of the case at all. So already, at this moment and after having struggled with the Milutinovic case for two years, I think are you pretty much on top of what you want to say against Mr. Djordjevic, and I see no reason why you should be unable, even given the time constraints and the pressure on your team, not to start now and be ready to hand down the -- the pre-trial brief in -- in two months from today. So I'm -- unless you have very convincing reasons, I will stick to the date that I have proposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see you're firm, Your Honour, but let me make one last pitch. How about Monday, the 25th? That gives us at least the weekend, those additional two days, that would still put us seven weeks before the proposed start of the trial date. That could make a big difference to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So, Monday, the 25th of August, it is. MR. HANNIS thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It is so decided, as we say in international negotiations. Thanks, Mr. Hannis. That leads me to the Defence team. And as I've already said, what we have in mind, is Monday, the 15th of September for you to file your pre-trial brief. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is not okay. However, I also have to explain why. It is not that we do not have sufficient funds or resources or staff. It is also -- we also have an issue with insufficient time, and I have to say when talking about the equality of arms in these proceedings, and I mean between the Prosecution and the Defence, we are in a rather bad position because Mr. Hannis's team, working on the current Kosovo case, is far more aware of the evidence and exhibits and they've also been on site, and I just have to say that the Defence, as I mentioned at the very beginning, and as I have been stressing here all the time, we wish to show respect for all participants in these proceedings but not to the prejudice to our client. The only thing that I can say is that I doubt that we will be able to fully prepare for the trial, which means that even if we were not to use our vacation time, we would not be able to prepare for the defence of our client by 15 September. So this is something that I fear and I have to -- when the Defence case is concerned, in such a complex case as this one. I'm not saying that Mr. Hannis is to blame that they are better prepared and they could begin with the trial as of tomorrow, but I'm afraid, Your Honour, that the Defence will not be able to provide a good defence by the dead-lines that you have set forth. And even with the pre-trial briefs and the times when they have to be submitted and the dead-lines that are to follow that, we will try to meet all our obligations within the dead-lines that you have envisaged. However, I have to say that I'm not fully -- I have not been able to form a full picture of the case and I have to say that my team has been very busy working very hard from the very start but we have a lot of problems with the lack of time for preparation of the Defence case. That's all that I would like to say, and it is absolutely not any wish on my part to obstruct these proceedings, because my client, too, would like to have the trial as soon as possible and justice served.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. I am sorry to hear that you feel that you are unable to prepare your defence within the time-limits that I have indicated, but I must also raise with you the issue that is on my mind; namely, that the flip-side of the Prosecution's work with the MOS case for two years is that for your client, most of the evidence that you know will be coming up in the trial against your client is known, in the sense that it has been already presented in the Milutinovic case. So you are in a much better position than most other of your colleagues, because they haven't seen the evidence. Now, in your case, you have seen the evidence, and so you have a much better idea of what is coming against you. Secondly, it is today, the 21st of June. The proposed date for the start of the trial -- sorry, the 20th of June. I'm always ahead of time. It is the 20th of June today. The proposed time for the beginning of the trial is mid-October. I have indicated a date, Monday, the 13th, in which I will consult with the President about -- I will consult the President about this date, and my expectation is that it is either going to be on Monday, the 13th of October or in the days immediately thereafter that the trial will actually start. That's four months from now. And so the trial date is actually four months ahead, which should give you ample time to -- to prepare. Your Defence pre-trial brief is then due one month earlier, that is, three months ahead from now. And also there, I think, that you have -- you're in a better position, as I said, than many of your -- your colleagues in other cases, Defence counsels in other cases, because you can always consult their pre-trial briefs, you can see what they had to say at the time and you can assist the evidence coming against Mr. Djordjevic. So I don't think that -- that you are in a terribly disadvantaged position to get pre-trial brief ready in three months from now and to be able to start trial in four months from now. So as I have been showing some sort of firmness with the Prosecution, I will have to do the same thing with the Defence, and I hope that given the circumstances and time you still available to you and the opportunity you have to acquaint yourself with much of the evidence which will be brought at trial against your client, at this moment I hope that you will be able to be ready to go to trial on that day. Would you wish to reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We cannot respond to the Trial Chamber, because the Trial Chamber is the one that is leading this case. So we are there to comply with whatever deadlines you set, no matter how much pain that may cause us. But I just have to say that the Defence of course did not expect to have any benefits that the Prosecution would not. We expect to have the same treatment, and of course that's the way that you have been leading this, and I don't expect that that will change. But I do need to stress again that we have not received all materials yet. I mean some confidential material. And we have submitted a motion where we stress this. This was immediately before the 65 ter meeting. So I have to say that the sooner we get this, the better we will be prepared. As for the advantage that you mentioned that we have as compared to our other colleagues in the Milutinovic, et al team or the Kosovo -- the Kosovo case, as it were, I do not wish to comment on that, because, of course, each Defence team has to deal with the situations that they're in, and we will do the same. And in any case, it is good that we have the information that the Prosecution had at its disposal in the previous case, but -- and we will have time to analyse these materials more than our other colleagues have had. And this would be all that I have to say, and I will end on this note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. Your remarks call me to make an observation about the impacts of the MOS judgement on this case, on our present case, because I, of course, understand immediately the logic that it would be nice to have the Milutinovic judgement handed down to us before we start trial. It would be nice to have the judgement before we submit the pre-trial briefs. It would be nice to have the Milutinovic judgement before we decide on which witnesses to call and which witnesses to call under 92 ter or bis or 65 ter. All these things would be very nice. But if we have to wait for the Milutinovic judgement to come down, then I think we will be in violation of Mr. Djordjevic's right to an expedient trial. Because the -- the reality is that although we might expect to get the Milutinovic judgement rendered before or maybe shortly after, I understand, maybe shortly after the opening of our trial, the likelihood is that the judgement might be appealed and then we will have to wait for another year or two, maybe not, but at least wait for some further time until finally the Appeal Chamber judgement is handed down. And if we were to wait for that to happen before we can begin the trial against Mr. Djordjevic here, I think it would be unreasonable and, as I said, a violation of his right to an expeditious trial. So that is why we had decided to simply get on with it and we will then have to make adjustments, if necessary, once we see the Milutinovic judgement. If that calls for any adjustment to the indictment against Mr. Djordjevic, then I suppose that the Prosecution will move for that or maybe you will wish to move for a further amendment of the indictment or that certain counts be stricken or something of that kind, but let's cross that bridge when we get there and not concern ourselves too much with it. I think that the important thing is that the trial against Mr. Djordjevic begins as soon as possible and there is, in my view, no reason to wait until we have the final decision from the Appeals Chamber, if eventually the Milutinovic judgement is appealed. So we have to start on the best possible foundation that we can, and then, if necessary, we'll have to make adjustments as we go along. That is as much as I would have to say about the beginning of the trial. Now, for the issue of witnesses, of course, under Rule 73 bis it is for the Trial Chamber and not for the Pre-Trial Judge to determine the number of witnesses and the number of hours allocated to hear each witness. By the way I intend to run this pre-trial is to prepare everything for the Trial Chamber so as to be able to present a draft decision to the Trial Chamber by the end of the pre-trial phase regarding the number of witnesses and the number of hours, because I'm in a better position now than the Trial Chamber will be in mid-October to discuss with the parties how many witnesses and especially discuss with the Prosecution how many witnesses you need and how much time you need for each of these witnesses. So for that purpose I would seek to invite you, both parties, to one or two 65 ter meetings in September. I don't think that it will affect in any way the Defence's preparation of its pre-trial brief because the number of Prosecution witnesses will have little impact on what you wish to put forward in your pre-trial brief. But in the month of September and -- I would wish to call you for a couple of internal 65 ter meetings, and the purpose of those meetings will be to sit down and have a look at your proposed list of witnesses and proposed time allocated to this. That will also have an impact on the estimated length of the trial. I understand that your case, including 20 per cent time set aside for administrative business and equal time for the Defence to do cross-examination, is somewhere between four and six months. And -- but we will have a much, much better idea when we see your witness list and have a chance to go through it. So in order to be in a position to recommend something to the Trial Chamber by the end of my pre-trial phase, I wish to consult the parties at that time, and I hope that you will be ready to go along with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think that will be very helpful, Your Honour. We can have a list in hand with number of projected hours for each witness and mode of testimony, and I think that will be useful to all of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right, I think so too. So Mrs. Murnane will call you to those meetings once we get closer to the time. I think that brings us more or less to the end of the agenda, and so what remains on my list is to address Mr. Djordjevic and, first of all, ask you Mr. Djordjevic, how are you doing? Are you in good health?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I don't have any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm very pleased to hear that, because if on top of the trial --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Me too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- if you were also to suffer medical or other kinds of problems, then it would be more than -- than I would wish for anyone. Is there, Mr. Djordjevic, any issue relating to your detention that we should look into?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Nothing at all. Everything is as usual, like for every other detainee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The next Status Conference will be held -- I don't know, Ms. Murnane, could you help us out here. It seems that the next Status Conference is just about the time when the trial is going to start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The next Status Conference, I'm told, will be on the 20th of October, which is a Monday, but that's on the very 120-day limit. So if the trial has not begun, which I expect that it will have begun in the week that begins with Monday, the 13th October, but if for any reason that the trial has not begun then, I anticipate that we will have the last Status Conference sometime in that week, between the 13th of October and the 17th of October. But, as I said, I suspect that the trial will have started by then. Do the parties have any other issues they wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Nothing from the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This concludes this Status Conference, and, as I said, I look forward to seeing the parties again for 65 ter meetings in September. This hearing is adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: [Trial Chamber and senior legal officer confer]
--- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
